lines.text: Squeeze a red grape... and the juice runs clear.
So where does Bordeaux get its deep, ruby red?
Bordeaux, in south-west France. Right on the forty-fifth parallel, the [Garonne](/ɡəɹˈɑːn/) and [Dordogne](/dɔːɹdˈɔɪn/) rivers meet, to form the [Gironde](/ʒiɹˈɑːnd/) estuary.
It splits the vineyards in two: the Left Bank... and the Right Bank.
On the Left Bank, deep gravel drains the rain and stores the sun's heat. Perfect for [Cabernet Sauvignon](/kˌæbɚnˈeɪ sˌoʊvɪnjˈɑːn/).
On the Right Bank, cooler clay and limestone favor [Merlot](/mɚlˈoʊ/).
[Merlot](/mɚlˈoʊ/) is the region's most planted red grape, with [Cabernet Sauvignon](/kˌæbɚnˈeɪ sˌoʊvɪnjˈɑːn/) and [Cabernet Franc](/kˌæbɚnˈeɪ fɹˈɑːŋk/) close behind.
Through the summer, the berries turn from green to purple. Sugar climbs, acidity falls...
and in September, the harvest begins. Often by hand, into small crates.
At the winery, the grapes are sorted, destemmed, and gently crushed.
Inside the vat, yeasts turn sugar into alcohol, and carbon dioxide.
And here's the answer. The color lives in the skins.
For up to a month, the juice soaks with them, drawing out pigments called [anthocyanins](/ˌænθoʊsˈaɪənɪnz/), along with tannins.
The new wine is pressed off the skins, and a second fermentation softens its sharp [malic](/mˈælɪk/) acid.
Then it rests in French oak [barriques](/bəɹˈiːks/), two hundred and twenty-five liters each, for twelve to twenty-four months.
Oak lets in tiny amounts of oxygen, rounding the tannins, and adding notes of vanilla, toast and spice.
Then comes Bordeaux's signature art: the blend. Left Bank wines lean on [Cabernet Sauvignon](/kˌæbɚnˈeɪ sˌoʊvɪnjˈɑːn/). Right Bank wines, on [Merlot](/mɚlˈoʊ/).
Once bottled, the finest vintages can keep evolving for decades.
Sun, soil, skins and oak. That's the red of Bordeaux.
